seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: I leave Locarno today. My address in Zurich for the moment will be c/o sig. Ugo Moggi, Friedaustrasse 7, Zurich. It was not possible to remain on here as I have no lessons to supplement my income and my New York publisher writes that the sales of my novel have come to a standstill. It is a miracle that I managed to remain here nearly three months. I am not delighted to return to Zurich where the temperature is 16 below zero and there is lack of everything, including coal. However I have no choice. The business of looking for & finding some tolerable quarters will take up some of my time and may delay for a week or so the sending of the third episode of the Telemachia. I suggest, however, that you print the whole first episode in one number & the second in the next. I confirm my postcard and repeat here the corrections on the typescript which I beg you to forward at once to the Little Review and Egoist .
I am sure there are other mistakes. My bad eyesight and the condition in which my typing is done are to blame.
I hope you got my postcard. If not, let me thank you for your kind words about my book. I am very grateful to you for your encouragement. In haste.

div.note: JJ wintered with his family in Locarno, a Swiss town on the northern shore of Lake Maggiore. Nora Barnacle with their two children, Lucia and Giorgio, had gone ahead in July 1917, but she returned to Zurich after JJ suffered renewed symptoms of glaucoma after an attack of lumbago there on 18 August. Once he had sufficiently recovered from eye surgery, he and the family went to Locarno in October 1917 and stayed there until January 1918. At first they stayed at the Pension Villa Rosa, then moved in mid-November to the Pension Daheim (Ellmann, JJ 417-18).
B.W. Huebsch of New York published the first edition of JJ’s A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man on 29 December 1916, priced at $1.50 a copy.
In January 1918, JJ and family found quarters at Universitätsstrasse 38 in Zurich.

“Proteus” is the third and final episode of the “Telemachia,” part one of Ulysses. As JJ finished the early episodes, he had them typed in Zurich and sent on to Pound in London, who reviewed and forwarded them to New York where they were printed in serial form in The Little Review, edited by Margaret Anderson and Jane Heap.

Pound had initially thought that “Telemachus,” running to seventeen pages in typescript, might be broken into three installments for The Little Review (Pound/Joyce 129), but the episode appeared entire in the number for March 1918. “Nestor” and “Proteus” were printed in the numbers for April and May 1918, respectively.
Possibly JJ to Pound, 1 January 1918, in which JJ requested a correction to the typescript of the “Nestor” episode.

Only a few episodes of Ulysses – “Nestor,” “Proteus,” “Hades,” and part of “Wandering Rocks” – appeared in the London magazine The Egoist during 1919, because the editor, Harriet Shaw Weaver, had difficulty finding a printer who would risk producing even these relatively tame portions of the book (Ellmann, JJ 443).

In “Telemachus,” as Buck Mulligan takes Stephen Dedalus’s arm and converses with him atop the tower they are staying in, Stephen thinks: “Cranly’s arm. His arm” (Little Review, vol. 4, no. 11 [March 1918]: 7; U 1.159). This recalls the serious discussions that Stephen had with his university friend Cranly in A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man. As they walked about Dublin, talking of religion and other subjects, Cranly occasionally took or touched Stephen’s arm (P 238, 239, 241, 247). Stephen suspects that Cranly and Mulligan are not sincere friends.

In “Telemachus” as published in The Little Review and later in the 1922 edition of Ulysses, an old woman arrives to deliver milk as Stephen, Mulligan, and Haines eat breakfast in the tower. She asks Mulligan if he is a medical student. “I am, ma’am, Buck Mulligan answered” (Little Review, vol. 4, no. 11 [March 1918]: 14; U 1922 14). The phrase “Look at that now, she said,” which JJ here asks Pound to insert after Mulligan’s words, did not make it into The Little Review or the 1922 Ulysses, but was restored in the 1984-1986 Gabler edition of Ulysses (U 1.415-17).

In “Telemachus,” as Stephen, Mulligan, and Haines leave the tower, Stephen says to Haines, possibly in reference to frequent hangovers: “I’m always tired in the morning” (Little Review, vol. 4, no. 11 [March 1918]: 18). In the 1922 edition and later editions, this was changed back to “We’re always tired in the morning” (U 1922 18; U 1.562).
Probably Pound’s praise for “Telemachus” in his letter to JJ dated 19 December 1917 (Pound/Joyce 128-29).
